proposition.claim:
Throughout, \(X\) is smooth and projective over \(\mathbb C\), \(A\) is ample and globally generated, and \(L_m=\mathcal O_X(K_X+mA)\). Theorem 1.2 states \(N_p\) for \(m\ge n+1+p\); Theorem 1.4 states Koszulness for \(m\ge n+2\). Section 2 explicitly permits \(N_p\) for globally generated line bundles without requiring an embedding. Consequently \(X=\mathbb P^n,A=\mathcal O(1),m=n+1\), where \(L_m=\mathcal O\), is not a counterexample to the stated \(N_0\) convention.

A basepoint-free subspace of dimension \(n+1\) gives a finite flat map \(\alpha:X\to\mathbb P^n\). The enlarged diagonal is \(\Gamma_X=X\times_{\mathbb P^n}X\); it contains \(\Delta_X\), and its extra components meet the ordinary diagonal over the branch locus. The star arrangement \(\Delta^1\) uses edges \((1,j)\); the chain arrangement \(\Delta^2\) uses edges \((j-1,j)\). These are different ideals and serve different criteria.

The proof establishes vanishing for the enlarged arrangements in Theorem 5.8, with thresholds \(m\ge n+r-1\) for stars and \(m\ge n+2\) for chains. It then needs surjectivity of restrictions from enlarged to ordinary arrangements. The invariant construction on p. 15 and its reuse on p. 17 are the bridge to this required surjectivity; they are not consequences of Theorem 5.8 alone.

Canonical second-factor G action makes restriction to direct sum of graph components an isomorphism on invariants, hence transports arbitrary diagonal sections into regular sections of Gamma.
